Mr. Cetina said that: "After reading the entire paragraph, it was noticeable the last sentence of the paragraph did not refer to the very content of this paragraph, and the context is misleading." So your correction is that, as it stands, your statement indicates -- to the OTP indicates that -- the passage "I would agree that once the Serbs had fled from the liberated area, the area was under the control of the Croatian armed forces" was in relation to the crimes that you had been discussing, whereas you have now, over the last couple of weeks, said that that passage was not provided in the context of the crimes you were discussing. So can you then tell us in what context did you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. However, based on the answer that you have just now quoted to me, I would say that the question must have been leading in this way. And I'm really sorry that we don't have the question here. We don't have the substance of the question, and that would help us to see why this was put in the context as it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, if you cannot recall the context in which you said it, how is it that after seven years, after you made the statement to the OTP, you could now tell this Trial Chamber that that particular sentence was not made within the context in which that sentence is recorded presently? On what basis did you make that correction?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis that it simply does not fit with the rest of the paragraph of the statement. I had besides an hour to review the entire statement and to state whether I was in agreement with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Why didn't you notice that when you initially reviewed the statement in April, the initiate contact you had with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have overlooked it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me take you to the third correction you made and that's a correction to page 14 of the OTP statement, paragraph 6. And referring to -- there, you refer to meetings hosted by Mr. Cermak. This is what you say in your OTP statement: "Cermak hosted these meetings, but they were not very formal, and there was no specific agenda. We were all given the opportunity to outline our problems, but no specific decisions were made. Everybody had to resolve their own problems, and nobody could issue an order to anybody else. These meetings were, in fact, only an opportunity to communicate with each other. General Cermak must have been aware of ongoing murders because he had to ask for reports." You have made a correction to that, and it is a clarification. You say that: "Mr. Cetina said that he explained in the statement to the Defence they concerned the exchange of information about events in Knin because the civil police was interested in the functioning of matters in the civilian area, such as restoring electricity, water, cleaning of the town, protection of economic facilities, factories, et cetera ..." And you further clarify what those meetings were about. Now, do I understand this correction to mean that you -- what you're saying here is that those meetings were conducted between Mr. Cermak and yourself for purposes of discussing administrative matters such as restoring electricity and waterworks, or were other issues also discussed at these meetings such as crimes and the problems that were faced by civilian police and police in the area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Mr. Cermak had such information, we would gladly have accepted it. We were talking about the setting up of an office to deal with state administration matters such as the settlement of domicile issues, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, that's not my question, Mr. Cetina. My question is: At those meetings between yourself and Cermak - and I believe you also say that Mr. Franjo Djurica also attended those meetings sometimes - did you also discuss, apart from, you know, waterworks and electricity -- the restoration of electricity and such matters, did you also discuss crimes that were being committed in your area and the problems? Did you inform Mr. Cermak the problems that your police officers had in policing the area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have the obligation to inform Mr. Cermak. In principle, we primarily went to the Knin police station and then afterwards we would go to see Mr. Cermak --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, please --

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please, go ahead. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, if Mr. Cermak had certain information about events that were of interest to the police, then we gladly heard him out on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, the questions are pretty clear, that is: Did you discuss the occurrence of crime and problems you may have had in coping with that during these meetings? Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we did; however, I -- our primary interest lay with the policing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would have said "yes" approximately three minutes ago, then we would have known your answer immediately rather than whether there was an obligation to do so, whether that if Mr. Cermak had certain information that you would have been willing to receive that. Let's try to stick to the facts. The questions were clear. And could you please directly answer the questions that are put to you by Ms. Mahindaratne. You may proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, let me take you to another part of your statement made to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could D1745 on the screen. This is at page 5, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You refer to the police commanders appointed in your area of responsibility and you say: "I believe that all or most of the police officers who were appointed as station commanders were Serbs," the fifth line on paragraph 3. And the second line above that you say: "They also made appointments of professional police officers who were called coordinators." Now, isn't it correct that the reason why the police commanders who appointed were of Serb ethnicity was the constitutional requirement which made it mandatory for appointment of persons of Serb ethnicity in areas which were predominantly inhabited by Serbs? Wasn't that the reason why the police commanders in your area of responsibility were all Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry appointed them, and I presumed that that was the reason, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now -- and since this was liberated territory and as such these were areas which were predominantly inhabited by the Serb population, therefore this was to fulfil that particular constitutional requirement; isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the police coordinators who were appointed. Isn't it correct that all the police coordinators were of Croatian ethnicity -- I'm sorry, Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they were Croats. I would have to look at their background information. They were all appointed by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Buhin, one of the police coordinators?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: He was of Croat ethnicity; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume so. I don't know how he declared himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, is there any dispute about the ethnical background of police coordinators?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I was just addressing paragraph -- I will move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kay asked you a series of questions yesterday as to if advanced preparations had been taken prior to Operation Storm to set up police work in the liberated areas --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is at transcript reference 23.397 to 23.398.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that prior to Operation Storm there were a series of military operations going even back to 1993 - and I'm referring to Operation Medak Pocket and in 1995 there was Flash - where territory formerly held by the RSK were liberated?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were liberated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So isn't it correct then that the officials of the Ministry of the Interior did have previous experience in preparing for policing of liberated territory as a consequence of the previous operations?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, but we didn't. At the time, I was not in a position that would permit me to plan that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me, Mr. Cetina, that crimes were committed in the liberated territories after those previous operations too?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details. I know what I could read in the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what did you read in the media? Does that confirm -- what you read in the media, does that confirm my proposition to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duties were not of such a nature that would permit me to have information about what was happening in the areas. Whatever I knew was what I could read in the press, and I can't go in the details. I know that there were certain judgements in connection with this. That's the extent of the knowledge I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, the only thing Ms. Mahindaratne asked you is what you did read in the newspapers, because your previous answer referred her to newspapers. Now, did you read in those newspapers that crimes were committed in the liberated territories in these earlier stages of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read that in connection with Medak Pocket there were judgements rendered which had to do with General Norac. I wasn't aware of anything other than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just then seek -- the only thing you read about what happened -- well, first of all, there were two operations referred to by Ms. Mahindaratne, the first Medak Pocket, the second Flash. When reading the newspapers, it was only that you read about General Norac -- judgement against General Norac being rendered, or did you ever read something about crimes that may have been committed at the time in the Medak Pocket where an operation had taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, only about the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And about Flash, Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall reading anything specific about any judgements in connection with Flash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't asking about judgements but about crimes reported about having been committed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't remember. I would have to peruse the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, your testimony - and I'm here referring to D1745, page 6, paragraph 1 - that you conducted daily meetings with the police commanders within your area of responsibility and the police coordinators and that you also took field trips to check on the ground situation. Now, those police commanders you met with on a daily meetings would include Mr. Romanic and Mr. Mihic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't meet with everyone every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Whom did you meet with at your daily meetings of the police -- your police commanders? Would you have a representative from the Knin police, either Mr. Romanic or Mr. Mihic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you'll allow me to, I'll explain this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the vast territory and the lack of communications, several days later the need arose for different police stations to be visited on different days. If you had five to six police stations, you could set aside one day for each of the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So it would be correct to say that you met with Mr. Romanic and/or Mr. Mihic regularly, if not daily?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On average, once a week with Mr. Romanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you also met with the police coordinators, Mr. Buhin and Mr. Baric, who were -- who oversaw the area Knin and the related area on a regular basis, did you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met them less often than I did Mr. Romanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At those meetings, were crimes and the problems the police had in the area in policing the crimes discussed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All manner of problems were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did the police commanders give you a report of the reports of crimes the police stations had received or the area the police administration in the case of Knin police administration had received in a given time and what follow-up investigation steps had been taken in relation to those matters?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They reported to me on the most important issues. I could not have possibly been aware of all the matters. Steps were taken through the chiefs that were subordinated to me, either in relation to the ordinary uniformed police, criminal investigation police, or the civilian protection department.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to your statement given to the OTP --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that's -- I'm sorry, statement given to the Defence, that's D1743 -- that's correct, D1743. Mr. Registrar, if I could have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And there in paragraph 17 - this is in relation to the incident in Grubori, Mr. Cetina - this is what you say: "I found out about the murders in the village of Grubori later, because I was not in my office on the day when the murders occurred or for several days afterwards." About five lines below that you say: "Mr. Kardum informed me about those events a day or two after they happened. When he informed me about all the events, he told me that coordinators Buhin and Baric from the Knin District Police Administration were informed immediately about those events and that they immediately reported to their superiors in Zagreb. Therefore, my further engagement regarding the events in Grubori was unnecessary." Now, after Mr. Kardum informed you about the incident in Grubori, did you inquire from him at any stage thereafter as to the status of that investigation as to whether any perpetrators have been arrested?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum informed me of the incident which took place in Grubori and told me precisely what you've mentioned now, that Buhin and Baric had been informed about everything. I believed that Mr. Romanic was aware of it as well. As for the follow-up action, I was not in Knin at the time. I was attending different -- I was attending to different tasks which took me to the north of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cetina, until when were you -- when did you hold the position as head of the police administration Knin-Zadar?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the head until the 31st of December, 1995, but as of January 1 of that year, I no longer performed the duties of the head as such.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The end of the witness's answer was unintelligible, could he please be asked to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, could you repeat the last bit of your answer that has not been taken down by the interpreters. Could you repeat what you just said.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 1st of December, I was -- I knew I was going to go back, and I went on leave. The deputy chief of the police administration took up my duties from that point on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Cetina, this incident, Grubori incident, occurred on 25th of August. Now, is it your position that after you were informed of the incident by Mr. Kardum some days after the incident, you never inquired from him as to the status of that investigation or as to if anybody has been arrested? You just completely ignored the matter thereafter? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not ignore that, but there were many events. Mr. Kardum informed me that it involved an incident which fell within the area where there were war operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, were -- did Mr. Kardum inform you that the incident related to the killing of five civilians and burning of several houses in a village?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly the number of persons involved, but, in any case, all the people who dealt with the incident had sufficient experience to know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Cetina, is: Do you consider that as a serious enough incident to inquire from your subordinate officers as to what action, follow-up action, had been taken by them? This is after all your area of responsibility in which a serious crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that this was probably a border-line case, he may have informed me or maybe Mr. Romanic did. I never wrote down what they actually told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "border-line case"? Can you clarify that? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This incident took place in Grubori, and for me at the time it was the only incident of that sort. That's why I referred to it as a border-line incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any written reports about the investigation regarding Grubori from your police officers, either Mr. Bitanga or Mr. Kardum or Mr. Romanic or Mr. Mihic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that. But if there are any documents attesting to that, please show them to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, there aren't any documents that we are aware of, Mr. Cetina. But are you -- to your knowledge, was an on-site investigation carried out into those killing incidents in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not. But it could be qualified as such only if there were measures taken under the law, although I don't think they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Cetina. I don't understand that answer. I asked you if -- so your -- do I just take your answer to be just "no"? But I don't understand what you meant by "but it could be qualified as such only if there were measures taken under the law ..." Do I understand your answer to be that there were no measures taken at all under the law in relation to that incident? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If such steps were taken and if there are documents in existence showing that, I would kindly ask to be shown those documents; otherwise, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, isn't it correct that Mr. Buhin, in fact, discussed this incident with you? He informed you about the killing incident? And in fact -- in fairness to you let me tell you exactly what Mr. Buhin said about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is, for the record, transcript reference 9981 to 82.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When Mr. Buhin, the police coordinator, was questioned about this incident this is what he said. He said: "I believe it was sufficient to inform the chief of the police administration, Mr. Ivica Cetina, and I'm sure he knew about what was going on. He promised that he would set up a team for an on-site inspection and make sure there was an investigating judge there. He also promised to dispatch them to Knin. At this point, there was no further need for me to check whether he had in fact done that or had informed the chief of the crime police." And at transcript page 9994 to 9995 this is what he said: "At the time, I informed Mr. Cetina about the incident and he spoke about dispatching an investigating judge and some forensic technicians. I had the impression that he was taking this seriously and that he would act based on this. He said that it would take him at least three hours to put together a team, get an investigating judge on the case, and for them to then reach Knin." Now, how do you respond to Mr. Buhin's testimony? According to him you -- he had discussed this incident with you, you were the person who were supposed to inform the investigating judge, and you were the person who was supposed to form a team to conduct an on-site investigation, none of which had happened. So can you explain to the Trial Chamber exactly your position on this matter.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly do not remember Mr. Buhin calling me and presenting the problem to me in such words. It is strange because Mr. Buhin was not subordinated or answerable to me. Why would he call me? He was supposed to call the ministry directly to state his opinion about the event. He could have called the state attorney's office and no one would have stopped him. He could have called Mr. Kardum and conveyed to him, since he was the chief of the crime police administration. Mr. Buhin was a coordinator who was directly appointed from the Ministry of the Interior, and as such was not subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence to mean that you can't recall Mr. Buhin telling you about this incident? Is that how I am to understand it? You don't have a recollection, is that what ...?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that recollection. It would not have been customary for Mr. Buhin to communicate with me in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, your earlier answer was: "I truly do not remember Mr. Buhin calling me and presenting the problem to me in such words." I now understand that you have no recollection that Mr. Buhin called you on the matter. What was the use of saying that you didn't remember him calling you "and presenting the problem to me in such words," which suggests that he may have done so in other words? Do you remember any conversation with Mr. Buhin on the Grubori incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not. It is only possible that Mr. Romanic informed me because I communicated with him far more extensively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of Mr. Romanic informing you about the Grubori incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that he informed me about the incident, but I believe - at least as far as I can recall - that I was informed about it by Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you say it's possible but you just don't remember that you -- that Mr. Romanic talked with you about the incident. Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cetina, you said that you -- to your knowledge no investigation -- or that you were not aware of an investigation or you were not aware of an investigating judge visiting this -- the scene of crime in Grubori. Now, when did you know that? At what stage did you know that no investigations had been carried out into the Grubori incident?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no investigations. As for when I learned of that, I could only give you an opinion of mine if I were shown a document but not from what I can remember alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, I'm trying to understand your position. You're the head of the Knin-Zadar Police Administration. In your area of responsibility, a serious crime has been committed: Five civilians and several houses burnt. And you, yourself, you are testifying that no investigations have been carried out into that incident, yet you have done nothing about it. Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber why you, as the head of the police force for that area, did not do anything to investigate a serious crime such as what happened in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information we have from the field was that the incident took place in a combat area; therefore, I had to receive information from different people, from all those who were in the field. And that information was put together by Mr. Kardum who informed me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you able to offer any plausible explanation to the Trial Chamber as to why your police officers, your subordinate police officers, didn't carry out any investigation into this incident?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the field and they were the best persons to assess what needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have - and this next document is under seal - it's D179.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have to go in private session or is there no need to do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No need, Mr. President, as long as the document is not shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: D179 is actually an exhibit the Chamber, in September 2008, inquired with the parties whether it needed to remain under seal. The Gotovina Defence had asked for it initially at the beginning of this case. We advised the -- Mr. Registrar that we no longer need it under seal and the Prosecution also took the same position, and therefore we would move that the status be changed and that it can be a public document. And I have the e-mail chain of communications in September 2008 if it's needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- the problem is to lift the confidential characteristic of an exhibit, not having a clear recollection why it was granted, is a bit beyond what the Chamber can do at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can state it briefly, Mr. President. It was at the beginning of the case and there was some discussion about the identity of victims being broadcast; however, the Prosecution has, subsequent to that, filed its clarification schedule of killing victims. That's a public document. And I think the parties agree that there is no longer a need to maintain that confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, relying primarily on your explanation and noting that none of the other parties have contradicted it, which I would not expect them to do because the Chamber is used to you informing the Chamber appropriately on matters in which the Chamber is seeking your assistance, then under those circumstances and having heard your explanation, D179 -- the Chamber changes the status of D179 in a public exhibit. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm also looking at the clock. Apparently -- I don't know how many questions you have on the next document. If it would be --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's -- it could be a substantial number of questions, Mr. President, so this might be a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we better first take the break. We'll have a break and resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, now this document was shown to you yesterday by Mr. Kay, you may recall, and when Mr. Kay asked you whether you recall this document being given to you by Mr. Elleby, you said you recalled receiving it and then you went on to say that the killings listed in this document were within your police administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the record, this is at page 23.450.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then you were asked as to what you did about this list, having received it from Mr. Elleby, and your answer was - and this is at page 23.450 - you said: "First of all, I have to say that it's a list of persons who quite certainly lost their lives during the war operations or most of them, and you can see that if you look at the dates when they were found. Part of those persons were certainly murdered as well, that is to say the crime of murder had been committed against them." Now, you didn't quite give an answer as to what you did after you received this list, but when you said that this document contains a list of persons who for the most -- most of whom have died during war operations, did you mean that the persons listed there had died due to combat activity and not -- they were not outright murdered? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could just go to the next page perhaps so that Mr. Cetina can have a reference to the list itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You looked at this list and that was the answer you gave.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you were asked as to what you did after receiving this list, your response was: "First of all, I have to say that it's a list of persons who quite certainly lost their lives during the war operations or most of them and you can see that if you look at the dates when they were found." Now, I have to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please then quote the whole of the answer in view of the question you just phrased. Mr. Cetina, you then said: "Part of those persons were certainly murdered as well, that is to say the crime of murder had been committed against them." That's the whole of the answer, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, looking at this document, what information led you to conclude that these persons had, in fact, died due to combat activity -- in fact, not all persons, you said "most of them" and that some had been murdered. What is it -- what information do you gather from this document which led you to give that response? Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do. A piece of information we had was the date of death, that is, the 5th of August. Next, could we please see the rest of the document. I think we also have some people from Varivode. I'm not sure, but perhaps we could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it may be of assistance if we show the witness the hard copy of the document so that he could go through it in entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I don't think I have a hard copy of the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But let me ask you this in order to make things -- to move on. Mr. Cetina, you said it was a date -- you said: "Quite certainly lost their lives during the war operations or most of them. And you can see that if you look at the dates when they were found." Now, you just mentioned 5th August. There was only one body found on 5th August. There isn't any other -- in this list, you can go through the entire list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Registrar, we could go page by page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I could not find any bodies found during the initial days of Operation Storm here which would lead you to conclude that, perhaps three or four at the most. Now, why did you say that most of these persons were killed as a result of war operations? What is it that you see in this document which would lead you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed in the area of war operations. That was the main reason why I made that conclusion. I don't know what other indicators there may be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So is it your position, Mr. Cetina, that any body found, person killed in the area where there had been war operations would lead the police to conclude immediately that they had died due to combat activity and then proceed on that basis? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right conclusion can be only made by the people, the teams who were in the field who had access to the scene and the right information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you would agree, then, that when you received this list you had to inquire as to if investigations had been conducted into each of these incidents to verify as to what the cause of death was and if it was, in fact, murder, that perpetrators were found or investigations were conducted; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that this document was forwarded to the chief Kardum of the crime police, and he had to correlate the persons and the locations and to link up with the civilian protection in order for sanitisation to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was that your primary interest, that sanitisation could be carried out? Were you not interested in finding out if, in fact, these matters had been investigated?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forwarded the document to the chief of the crime police and he knew what he had to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, let me tell you in fact what Mr. Kardum - he in fact testified in these proceedings - as to what he said about this list. Now, this is at transcript page T9511 going to 12. Mr. Kardum testified, and I'll read it to you. It was his testimony that you discussed this matter with him. And let me just --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: He testified that you discussed -- you and him, that you gave him the list, that you discussed the content, and it was sent on to Mr. Nadj of the Ministry of the Interior. Now, there was -- he did not say that you asked him to inquire into any investigations. There is no evidence at all supporting what you're saying here. Now, did you or didn't you make inquiries, either from Mr. Kardum or any other officers about it, as to whether these killing incidents had been investigated?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were incidents that happened in the war-affected areas. In my view, Mr. Kardum acted properly by sending the information to the Ministry of the Interior in order for them to make the right assessment about what could be done about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: As I understand your testimony, is it your position then that when you received information about persons killed in your area of responsibility from the international monitors, what you did was send that information to the Ministry of the Interior for the officials of the ministry to take -- make an assessment as to what should be done. Is that how you proceeded with matters?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum and Mr. Nadj, they were the heads of the crime investigation police, Mr. Nadj in Zagreb and Mr. Kardum in Zadar, and they were the most competent persons and the best-placed persons to decide about what had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Weren't you as the head of the police administration concerned as to finding out what was going on? Or did you just leave it in the hands of the subordinate officers without making further inquiries?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left it up to them to take the case further.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, in fact, when this list was shown to you by the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor - and I will take you right to that point in your statement. This is at page 10 of the OTP statement, paragraph 3 going onto 4 - when the list was shown to you this is what you said, this was in 2002: "I cannot be sure if I have ever seen that document. I had a lot of documents passing through my hands. I cannot recall if I ever responded to this letter from Jan Elleby." Now, in 2002 when you were shown this list, you couldn't -- you didn't have any recollection of that or that's what you claimed at that time. Then yesterday and today you clearly remember the list. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber as to why, when the investigators confronted you with this list in 2002, you didn't remember anything about it? Was there any reason why you wanted to distance yourself from this list?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no special reason for it; rather, they showed me the documents so speedily that I could not really concentrate at the time and realise whether I had seen it or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, in fact Mr. Elleby testified in these proceedings, and he -- his testimony was that when he handed over this list to you, you read the list, you put it aside, and asked Mr. Elleby to leave your office. This is at transcript reference T3377 as well as P216, page 5. Now, can you explain to the Trial Chamber as to why you reacted in that manner when Mr. Elleby gave you this list? Why were you hostile to Mr. Elleby when you were presented with this list?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In full respect of Mr. Elleby who stated something like that, that's absolutely not the truth. I'm not the kind of person who would throw anyone out of my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have document P53, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to your statement given to the Defence, and I just -- since we're going to have another document on the screen, let me read that to you. This is paragraph 10 of the Defence statement D1743. You were shown the document that will come on your screen which is now on your screen, and this is what you say about the document. You say: "I confirm that I have not seen this document before. I have already explained that a military serviceman could not issue orders to the police. From the aspect of the regulations on the police, there is no basis to be found anywhere in the law for the issue of any sort of military orders for the police station in Knin to which this order was sent. It was only information in terms of where the UNCRO staff would be moving, but this does not relate to the actions by the police." Now, as I understand your testimony to be, is it your, then, opinion that this was an order issued to the military police but sent to the civilian police for information. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about the military police. As for the civilian police it -- the order definitely didn't mean anything to the civilian police because the civilian police acts in keeping with the Law on Internal Affairs and Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this order, Mr. Cetina, you say this, that: "This order does not relate to any actions by the police." Now, isn't it correct that there were civilian police check-points established in the liberated territory?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So isn't this order -- before that, let me ask you one more question. Isn't it correct then that the UNCRO vehicles were stopped at those civilian police check-points?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the UNCRO vehicles were not stopped by the civilian police for checks or simply because they would not let them through.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is it your position that UNCRO vehicles were not stopped by civilian police check-points; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it should be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have D499, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, may I remind you that when something is asked about what happened, that the answer should not be what should have been done but what, as far as you know, happened. When you were asked whether it's correct that UNCRO vehicles were stopped at those civilian police check-points you said: "In my view, UNCRO vehicles were not stopped by the civilian police for checks ..." And then when Ms. Mahindaratne asked you whether it is your position that they were not stopped, you said: "That's the way it should be ..." which is not necessarily the same as what happened. Could I invite you to clearly answer to questions, where you're asked about what happened, to tell us what you know about those events. And if you're asked about whether that was in accordance with how it should be, you can, of course, tell us or give an answer to that question as well but not to mix them up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, are you familiar with this document? It's an order sent by Mr. Moric and it's addressed to the chiefs of the police administration, including yourself? Do you recall receiving this document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the order reads as follows, it says: "In accordance with your assessment that the general security situation in liberated areas is such that it allows for unimpeded movement of people and goods as well as a gradual normalisation of life, there is no longer any need to restrict movement in those areas. "Consequently, do not restrict the movement of European Union monitors, UNCIVPOL members, or UNCRO members. Movements and itineraries of UNHCR convoys must be announced in advance." Do you know that what you just said was incorrect because, in fact, the civilian police have been involved in restricting the movement of the UNCRO members and other international monitors?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, the police had not been restricting it, not even before the date of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that Mr. Moric issued an order of this nature without any basis? I don't understand your testimony, Mr. Cetina. If the civilian police were not involved in restricting the movement of the international monitors, why would Mr. Moric have issued this order?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of the document is that we should not be restricting the movement of the vehicles of these institutions either, and he's not referring to any sort of document whereby the ministry would have banned these institutions from moving about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. Moving on to another area. If I could read to you a statement you made about General Cermak's authority in the statement given to the OTP, that is D1745.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, for the record, that's at page 6, the last paragraph, fourth line.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Going from the bottom you say: "I do not know," referring to General Cermak, "I do not know what his official position was in Knin at the time and in the aftermath of Operation Storm. It was my impression that he was coordinating the work of the town services, such as ensuring electricity, water-supply, and cleaning up the town. I do not know why somebody in the rank of general was appointed to this post except maybe because the military was still present there." And then in the statement given to the Defence and that's D1743, paragraph 4, you say this about Mr. Cermak's authority: "I think that Mr. Djurica told me that Mr. Cermak had been appointed the commander of the Knin Garrison, but I do not know what the duties of a garrison are because I am not familiar with the military structure." Now, did General Cermak discuss his authority with you at any time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you receive any instructions from the Ministry of Interior officials or the assistant ministers or from Mr. Jarnjak regarding General Cermak's appointment to Knin and as to what you had to do to vis a vis Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In your statement to the Defence at paragraph 8 you say this: "I was very clear when I told investigators of the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor that Mr. Cermak did not have authority over the police, nor could he influence the work of the police. My superiors were in Zagreb and I reported to them about my work. My subjective impression was that Mr. Cermak did not impose himself on the police. There are two key regulations governing the procedure of the police. The first is the Law on the Police, and the second, the Rules of Procedure of the police. If we were to look at all the regulations from 1990 to date, we would not find a single regulation that mentions in any way that the army can command the police." If I understand your testimony so far, I understand what you say about your assertions about Mr. -- General Cermak's authority to be based on your understanding of the police regulations, namely, that the military could not command the police. That is what you are generally saying. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case, formally and de facto.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you were shown a number of orders issued by General Cermak to the Knin police by the Defence team, including the previous order we looked at, P53. And in your statement there are a number of paragraphs. You have expressed your opinion about what you think those documents mean. Now, until the Defence showed you those documents, you had not seen them. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not seen them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At any time, did either Mr. Romanic or Mr. Mihic or for that matter even the police coordinators inform you that General Cermak had issued orders to the Knin police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But did either Mr. Romanic or Mr. Mihic complain to you that they were receiving orders and ask -- seek your advice as to how they should respond to those orders?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So as I understand, since you hadn't seen the documents until the Defence showed them to you, Mr. Romanic or Mr. Mihic had not discussed them with you, your opinions expressed in the statement given to the Defence about those documents are mere speculations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're absolutely not speculations. And if you'll allow me to, I'll try and explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am surprised at such a view that General Cermak was the superior of the police because from what we were able to see yesterday and today from a number of documents which arrived from the ministry to the police administration, it was clear who it was that the police administration was addressing. These documents testify to the vertical hierarchy of the Ministry of the Interior. When this is coupled with the Law on the Internal Affairs and the Law on Criminal Procedure, the matter becomes quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have document P509, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, if I could just read back to you a statement you made in the Defence statement, that's paragraph 14. Now, this is with regard to the document you'll see in a moment, P509. You say: "I confirm that I have not seen it before. The police had their regulations which described the manner of establishing the identity of persons moving around in a certain area. Speaking in principle, it was a war area and the Serbs could not have had Croatian personal documents. Therefore, a policeman at a check-point or when he came across some person otherwise would have asked for personal documents to establish the person's identity but would not have asked that person for a pass. The Law on Temporary and Permanent Residence on the basis of which the policeman would act, as far as I know, does not recognise passes as a document; it only recognises a personal identity document." Now, in this order, General Cermak orders that: "From 15th August, 1995, onwards, allow civilians unhindered entry into the town of Knin at all check-points of the military and civilian police on all access roads to the town. "Permit the civilians to enter the town of Knin without passes and carry out routine checks following the rules set out earlier. "This order enters into force immediately." And it's addressed to Knin police station and Knin military police. Now, if you say there was no requirement for passes to allow people to move around, do you know why -- what prompted General Cermak to issue this order? Are you able to say -- I know you haven't seen the document. Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not been aware of it. I will try to explain the format of a police order if you'll allow me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you're not aware of it, I don't want you to, you know, speculate, Mr. Cetina. Let me show you another document that might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, perhaps we can -- because the witness apparently wants to explain something. Would you want to tell us that the format of this order is not the usual police format for orders? Is that what you had on your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to all those who drafted the document, but such a document could not be issued by the police because the preamble of the document should contain the basis pursuant to which the document is issued --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. What could or could not have been done, your testimony, apparently, you wanted to give, was that this is not the format you would normally find in a police organisation. That's where Ms. Mahindaratne stopped you. Now being aware of this, please move on, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, can I have D496, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, you can see this document which is a document issued by Split-Dalmatia Police Administration and it's dated the same day as General Cermak's order, the 15th of August, and it's addressed to the Povratak staff and it reads as follows: "Visits and admission to the liberated areas. "We are very pressured by citizens and displaced persons who wish to visit the liberated areas (Knin, Drnis, et cetera). "We have been informed that the regular Split-Knin railroad line has been restored, which is being regularly announced through the media (radio, television), where citizens are informed that they have free transport on the said railroad line in the next ten days. This creates enormous pressure both at barrier check-points and in operations staff because citizens feel that they can travel without any problem on the said train. "Please give us urgent directions as to how we should act in this newly developed situation." And that's a document from your colleague, head of Split-Dalmatia Police Administration. Do you note on the top right-hand side there's a handwriting notation there that says: "Call the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration and say that Cermak will annul the passes today."

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So possibly you were, then, not aware of a process, a system that was applicable on the ground, which was that there were passes? And, in fact, your colleague, the head of Split-Dalmatia administration had called for this, and do you note that -- that you have not been aware of a system? Do you agree that this is a matter that you have not been aware of?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember it, but I don't think I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, let me also show you another document, Mr. Cetina, in fact, which will really perhaps demonstrate to you that what you're talking about in terms of these passes is completely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, before showing a document to the witness to tell him already that it shows that his previous testimony was inaccurate or his understanding was inaccurate is not the way in which I expect cross-examination to be done. You may put leading questions to the witness, but already to tell him what the finding will be if we look at the document would be a bit early, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have -- this is a document under seal, P510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I have document 504, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, you -- in fact, your testimony is that Mr. Cermak did not have any authority over the Knin police. Let me show you a document and ask you this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, what you see on your screen is an order issued by General Cermak dated 11th of October, 1995, and it's addressed to the Knin police station. And it goes on to say: "On the basis of demonstrated needs and in order to be more operative, I hereby order: "A part of the MUP officers with the Knin police station shall be temporarily transferred to the old grammar school building in Knin, Petra Krvavice Street, number 5. "This order shall enter into force immediately." Now, were you aware that General Cermak issued an order to transfer -- temporarily transfer officers from the Knin police station to another location?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain something. This sentence does not say that they were supposed to be moved out of the police station building in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- while the issue is not whether you understand every detail of the text and whether police was ordered to move out, Ms. Mahindaratne would like to know whether you were aware of this document called an order, whether you are aware that it was issued by Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember it. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge on what is described here which deals with a transfer of a part of the MUP offices to the old grammar school building in Knin? Are you familiar with that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, taking you to the statement given to the OTP, you described a particular incident - and this is at page 7, paragraph 1 - you say: "I remember that General Cermak called me on the telephone about a month after Operation Storm. He told me that at a village, I'm not sure of the location, he said he was there on his own initiative and that as the village had no power he had organised a generator. General Cermak also stated that members of the international organisations were present in the village when he handed the generator to the villagers. The same evening, General Cermak called me again on the telephone and reported an incident to me. He told me that two men in a vehicle had been to the village and stolen sheep and cattle. He told me that I had to do something immediately to punish the offenders. I do not remember if the generator was also stolen. I remember that the police stopped the vehicle near Sinj and that the sheep and cattle were returned to the villagers. I immediately alerted the local police commanders, and that was why the criminals were stopped." Now, my first question is: Do you recall if that village that he referred to was a place called Oton Bender?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the location referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in such instances when General Cermak made requests or instructed that investigations be carried out into specific incidents and when that was done, did you report back to him and say, "Well, General, that was carried out?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sure the witness has ever said that as described by my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please take care that what you put to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, let me rephrase my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- accurately reflects his testimony or his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in that given situation, when General Cermak called you and said that something had to be done immediately to punish the offenders and you contacted the local police commanders and you say that -- and that was why the criminals were stopped, did you report back to General Cermak that indeed something had been done regarding his complaint?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not obliged to inform him. I don't recall whether I did, but I was under no obligation to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I can have P2645, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the document you will see on the screen, it's not -- I'm not suggesting it's the same incident, it's probably another incident. But it is a document that has been copied to you too. It's dated 21st October, 1995, and it's copied to Zadar Knin police authority, attention of the chief, crime police division attention of chief, Knin command post headquarters, attention of General Cermak, and Split-Dalmatia police authority. It refers to an investigation subject, Plaintiff Luka Pasic, criminal act of aggravated theft, and refers to an investigation carried out into --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Refers to criminal -- an investigation carried out into case of theft of 56 heads of sheep. Do you recall receiving this report?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my apologies. I have read a portion of that document which is under seal, so a redaction may be called for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please prepare a redaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, are you able to explain to the Trial Chamber as to why this report has been submitted to the -- to Mr. Cermak? And it's a report issued by Mr. Gambiroza.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not have written this document in such a way, but this was probably to inform the addressees about the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, usually if I send someone a document that is for the purpose of him knowing the existence of that document. That is an answer that does not respond to what you were asked. The question is whether you have an explanation as to why this was sent to Mr. Cermak, which means why this information given by Mr. Gambiroza was sent to Mr. Cermak in view of the position of Mr. Cermak in relation to police activities. That is, as you certainly would have understood, was the core of the question. Could you understand that question, whether you have an explanation; if not, then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, isn't it correct that when investigations were carried out at the behest of Mr. Cermak, reports were indeed sent back to him to let him know that he is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I must object because again we're falling into the trap that started the previous line of questions, isn't it right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I make my submission -- my apologies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but there is something included is that this was a -- that this was an investigation which was made at the behest of Mr. Cermak. And as you earlier said - and I do understand what, perhaps, the issue was - you started your line of questioning where you may have assumed that what we find in the document is the same event as dealt with by Mr. Cetina in his statement. Now, once you had asked about it, about Oton Bender, then you yourself said, Well, even if it's not the same. So you can put such a question to the witness, which would be, perhaps, Mr. Cetina, that where you earlier in your statement said that at a certain moment - and I'm talking about the event with the generators and the report that was received on theft - that if under those circumstances Mr. Cermak expressed as a view that something had to be done about it and that in a situation which shows some similarity with the event that you stated about, whether it comes as a surprise that, under those circumstances, Mr. Cermak is informed about the action taken on this -- again, this event which shows at least some similarity with the event you described, whether or not it is the same. Could you please answer that question. If it does not come as a surprise, I think everyone will understand that; if you think it comes as a surprise, please explain it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did receive information. I don't recall any particular details. In any case, I received information from General Cermak; and given the urgency, because the assessment was that the perpetrators were getting away in a vehicle, the information was passed on urgently and the perpetrators were found. I am not familiar with any details, but I did forward that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it your conclusion - and I have to interpret your answer - that the event you described in your statement is the same as the event on which we here see a report being sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say that with any certainty. I don't recall any details or locations or anything else concerning this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we return back to the question that was put to you, that if Mr. Cermak expresses as his view that something should be done about it, would it be to be expected that he would then be informed about the action taken upon what he had said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed. I'm not saying that the matter has been fully explored, so I leave that in your hands, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, let me just in fact bring up another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could have, Mr. Registrar, P2656 -- I'm sorry, I have made a mistake. P2650. My apologies, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, isn't it correct that you yourself sent written reports to General Cermak on investigations carried out into incidents? In fact, you will see what you're looking at right now is one such report.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So do you agree with me that you yourself sent written reports to General Cermak on investigations carried out into specific incidents?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature, and I sent this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You have, in fact, in this document - and I don't want to waste time reading the entire thing, you can read it - you have given a description of what has been done at a crime scene and of cartridge cases found, et cetera. Now, you just testified that there was no obligation on your part to send reports to General Cermak on crime -- investigations into crime. If you had no obligation, why were you submitting written reports providing such detail about investigations to Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know, but this document probably has a history, a chain of events, a reason that it was drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, I'm not showing you a document written by someone else. This is a document signed by you, therefore you perhaps would be the only person who could tell the Trial Chamber as to why you sent this document.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember why I sent this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm looking at the clock. We have to stop. Earlier you said that the event on which this witness testified which included generators being brought to a village and that same evening a report of sheep being stolen was probably another one. I do not know yet. If any of the parties is aware of an event other than the one in Oton Bender where generators were provided to a village where that same evening the thefts of sheep was reported, the Chamber would like to be informed about it so that we are better able to assess the probability of whether what the witness stated covers the same event or a different event.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't probably -- perhaps said it wrong -- I didn't want to say "probably," but I said "perhaps." The reason was the testimony given by this witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I am fully aware why you didn't say that it was the same event on the basis of the evidence. I think you couldn't say that. But you said that probably it was another event. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I just rise on a different matter slightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a different matter. Then I would first like to instruct Mr. Cetina that he should not speak with anyone - and that's the same instruction as I gave yesterday - Mr. Cetina, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony. And we would like to see you back tomorrow morning, but tomorrow morning. If you would please follow Madam Usher. Could you please follow Madam Usher. We deal with another matter which is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just as a housekeeping matter, Ms. Mahindaratne indicated that we needed a redaction because P2645 was under seal, and I'm looking at the document and in e-court and it doesn't indicate that the document has any confidential status.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I wasn't referring to -- not P2645 but P510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need to -- the matter has been raised. Last matter, Ms. Mahindaratne, you asked for five sessions. Could you give us an estimate as to whether you think you could stay within the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it will be much shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Much shorter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I believe I will be able to finish within the first two sessions tomorrow.

utterances.text: Yes, which would make it four. Could the other parties, Mr. Kay, could you already --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there may be some re-examination. It won't be of an inordinate length --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, of course, inordinate or not, I'd like to know whether there's a fair chance that we could conclude the testimony of this witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will. It's just that we haven't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I'm not asking a final assessment, of course you can't give that. But, nevertheless, it's good to know what your impression is up to this moment is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm concerned because the present theme of questioning and there is evidence that indicates why this witness sent details of cases to Mr. Cetina. We've seen the document from the International Commission of the Red Cross. We've seen other documents and, of course, we have our bar table submission pending, which enables some documents in chains to be put together. This has been served on the Prosecution, and it's certainly a matter we would like cleared up so that exhibit numbers could be given to the documents within our bar table. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see your point; at the same time, Ms. Mahindaratne, of course, can test whatever evidence, whether it's there already, as she wishes. At the same time, Ms. Mahindaratne, if a witness testifies that people were -- had died during combat operations and then not to put to him that he said already that some may have been killed, just ignoring the whole difference between "during" or as you repeatedly put to this witness "as a result of," that's not what the witness said. The more accurate the reference to the -- what is already in evidence is, the more the convincing capacity of testing that evidence could be. Accuracy is something which is highly appreciated. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the matter we're just looking at here, the last document -- and I rise because it comes from the Prosecution database and it's been uploaded by us as a criminal report referring to this matter dated the 20th of September, 1995, when the murders were committed, it's 2D00784.
